question: How do I order custom poly tabs?
answer: Set your cut and tabs per set, type your tab text, choose your poly colors and ink, pick finishing options, then check out with live pricing. A free PDF proof follows before anything prints.
topic: How to Order Custom Poly Tabs Online (Step by Step)

question: Can poly tabs be printed with white ink?
answer: Yes. White ink is the right choice on dark poly like black or blue, where black ink would disappear into the stock.
topic: How to Order Custom Poly Tabs Online (Step by Step)

question: How long does poly production take?
answer: About 15 business days from the moment you approve your proof. Poly is screen printed rather than digitally printed, which is what accounts for the longer schedule.
topic: How to Order Custom Poly Tabs Online (Step by Step)

question: What does collated mean for index tabs?
answer: Collated means each set arrives complete and in order, tab 1 through the last tab, ready to drop straight into a binder.
topic: Collated vs. Uncollated Index Tabs — What's the Difference?

question: What are uncollated tabs used for?
answer: Uncollated tabs arrive as separate stacks by position — every tab 1 together, every tab 2 together. That suits high-volume assembly lines where sets are built in bulk.
topic: Collated vs. Uncollated Index Tabs — What's the Difference?

question: Which should I choose?
answer: Choose collated unless you are assembling binders in volume and have a process built around position stacks. Collated is what most offices want.
topic: Collated vs. Uncollated Index Tabs — What's the Difference?

question: How do I choose the right number of tabs for my dividers?
answer: Count the sections your document actually has, then match that to a tab cut. The cut is the fraction of page height each tab occupies, so a 1/5 cut gives five tabs across one bank, a 1/8 cut gives eight, up to 1/15. Most professional sets land between 8 and 12 sections. Choose the cut that fits your section count exactly rather than buying tabs you will leave blank — empty tabs read as an afterthought and make the index slower to scan. The free tab cut calculator turns a section count into the right cut and number of banks.
topic: How Many Index Tabs Do You Need? (A Quick Planner)

question: How do I choose the right size and color for index tabs?
answer: Size follows section count: the more sections, the smaller the cut, from 1/2 down to 1/15. Color follows how the document is used — one color per section makes a file navigable without reading the tabs, which matters when the person pulling it is in a hurry or unfamiliar with it. Tabzoola offers 19 Mylar colors and 11 poly colors, mixed freely within one set. On poly, white ink reads better than black on dark colors.
topic: How Many Index Tabs Do You Need? (A Quick Planner)

question: How do I work out how many tabs I need?
answer: Count the sections your document actually needs to separate. That count is your tabs per set — there is no need to round up to a stock number, because the set is made to order.
topic: How Many Index Tabs Do You Need? (A Quick Planner)

question: What happens if I need more tabs than the cut allows?
answer: The tabs step into banks. With a 1/5 cut and 12 tabs, the positions cycle through five across and repeat, so a reader still sees a clean staircase down the page.
topic: How Many Index Tabs Do You Need? (A Quick Planner)

question: Can I change the tab count after I start designing?
answer: Yes. Adjust the count in the designer and the layout and price update immediately, and nothing prints until you approve your proof.
topic: How Many Index Tabs Do You Need? (A Quick Planner)

question: How do I choose a custom tab supplier?
answer: Verify seven things before you order: the real minimum order, the true turnaround including the proof step, whether the proof is instant or queued, who actually manufactures the tabs rather than brokering them, where free shipping genuinely starts, whether pricing is published without a quote form, and whether the options your job needs — poly, white ink, high cuts, two-sided printing — exist in the online designer. Any supplier can win on one question; run the whole list.
topic: How to Choose a Custom Tab Supplier — A Buyer's Checklist

question: How can I tell if a tab vendor is a manufacturer or a reseller?
answer: Ask for the plant address and how long they have die-cut tabs there, then check the answer is specific and verifiable. A manufacturer names its building, its equipment and its history; a reseller talks about its network or its partners. Two more signals: technical questions (die geometry, stock weights, Mylar application) get answered directly rather than relayed, and the trade name traces to a real manufacturing entity — Tabzoola, for example, sells tabs made by its sister company under the same owner, Anselmo Die & Index, Inc., which has die-cut index tabs in Schaumburg, Illinois since 1993.
topic: How to Choose a Custom Tab Supplier — A Buyer's Checklist

question: What is a fair price for custom index tabs?
answer: Judge any quote against published figures: custom paper index tabs run roughly $1.08 to $9.70 per set across common configurations (5-10 tabs per set, 25 to 1,000 sets), with an 8-tab paper set at $8.00 per set at 25 sets falling to $2.44 at 250 — setup included. At Tabzoola, a 5-tab set is $5.45 per set at 25 and $1.57 at 250. If a supplier's number is far above that, ask what the difference buys; if the price only appears after a callback, it depends on the salesperson. Poly runs higher ($4.35 to $47.00 per set) because it is screen printed on .015 plastic.
topic: How to Choose a Custom Tab Supplier — A Buyer's Checklist

question: What minimum order is typical for custom tabs?
answer: Floors vary widely: some suppliers will not run fewer than 50 sets, others quote case quantities only. Twenty-five sets is the low end of the industry and is Tabzoola's minimum on both paper and poly. If you need a single binder's worth, no custom supplier is the right answer — use a printable template or a stock pack and switch to custom when the same set starts being reproduced.
topic: How to Choose a Custom Tab Supplier — A Buyer's Checklist

question: How long should custom tabs take?
answer: Measure from proof approval, not from payment — quoted production times usually start only when you approve the proof, so a proof that takes days to arrive extends the real wait invisibly. About 5 business days for paper and about 15 for poly from approval is the standard a buyer should expect; add shipping. Ask every supplier the same question: when does your clock start?
topic: How to Choose a Custom Tab Supplier — A Buyer's Checklist

question: Should I order custom tabs from a supplier that requires a quote form?
answer: A quote form is not disqualifying, but it changes what you can verify: unpublished pricing cannot be compared, checked at midnight, or written into a requisition without a callback, and procurement files built on a single quote fail price-reasonableness review more often than files built on published tables. Prefer suppliers whose per-set prices are public — whoever they are.
topic: How to Choose a Custom Tab Supplier — A Buyer's Checklist

question: Can a custom tab supplier handle purchase orders and vendor setup?
answer: The institutional buyers who order tabs in volume — districts, municipalities, hospitals, housing authorities — mostly cannot pay by card, so a supplier that only takes cards is a practical blocker. Ask whether they accept POs on Net-30 terms and routinely handle W-9s, vendor registration forms, certificates of insurance and tax-exemption certificates. Tabzoola treats an emailed PO as the order and invoices on Net 30 — the family firm behind it was founded in 1978 and has supplied index tabs on institutional terms since 1993.
topic: How to Choose a Custom Tab Supplier — A Buyer's Checklist

question: Does Tabzoola make its own tabs?
answer: Yes. Every order is printed, die-cut, Mylar-reinforced on every tab and collated at our own plant in Schaumburg, Illinois — Anselmo Die & Index, Inc., family owned since 1978, die-cutting index tabs since 1993. That is also the checklist's hardest question for any supplier to fake: the plant either exists or it does not.
topic: How to Choose a Custom Tab Supplier — A Buyer's Checklist

question: Do dividers go in front of or behind their section?
answer: In front — the divider is the section's cover page, and everything behind it belongs to that tab until the next divider. Filing a divider behind its pages is the single most common assembly mistake, and it makes every tab point at the previous section's contents.
topic: How to Use Tab Dividers: A Practical Guide

question: How should I organize binder tab dividers?
answer: Start with the reader, not the table of contents. Order and label the sections the way the person using the binder will look for them, and the labels mostly write themselves.
topic: How to Use Tab Dividers: A Practical Guide

question: When does color coding actually help?
answer: Color earns its keep when someone needs to find a section from across the room or at a glance under pressure. Coloring every tab differently for its own sake just adds noise.
topic: How to Use Tab Dividers: A Practical Guide

question: Should I use printed tabs or write-on tabs?
answer: Write-on tabs suit one-off binders that change often. Printed tabs are the better choice the moment the same set is reproduced, because every copy reads identically; Tabzoola prints sets like that from a 25-set minimum, with the titles on the tab itself.
topic: How to Use Tab Dividers: A Practical Guide

question: Can I write on the tabs of index dividers?
answer: On paper tabs, yes — the index stock is uncoated and takes permanent marker well (ballpoint less so), and a wider cut like 1/5 or 1/4 leaves room to write legibly. Poly tabs are the opposite: the wipe-clean surface that survives disinfectant is exactly what keeps handwriting from staying put. The full trade-off is in the write-on vs printed guide.
topic: How to Use Tab Dividers: A Practical Guide

question: What goes in a trial binder?
answer: Most trial notebooks use ten sections, in the order the trial runs: Case Summary, Pleadings, Motions & Orders, Jury Selection, Opening Statement, Witnesses, Exhibits, Jury Instructions, Closing Argument, and Law & Research. Exhibits usually go in a binder of their own, tabbed Exhibit 1 onward or by party prefix. Tabzoola's free trial binder builder starts with those ten sections ticked and prices the printed set: $9.92 a set at 25 sets for the ten-section notebook, and $22.99 a set for Exhibit 1 to 25, collated and 3-hole punched.
topic: Trial Exhibit Tabs: Numbering and Court Binders

question: Should exhibits be numbered or lettered?
answer: Both conventions are in use and the court or jurisdiction usually decides. Custom printing means you can follow whichever convention the matter requires, starting at any number or letter.
topic: Trial Exhibit Tabs: Numbering and Court Binders

question: How many sets of exhibit tabs does one trial need?
answer: Plan a set for the judge, opposing counsel, the witness stand, and your own table, plus spares. That is why the 25-set minimum tends to line up with a single significant matter.
topic: Trial Exhibit Tabs: Numbering and Court Binders

question: What do exhibit tabs need to survive?
answer: Repeated handling under pressure. Mylar reinforcement on the tab edge, or poly stock, keeps tabs from tearing away during a long trial day.
topic: Trial Exhibit Tabs: Numbering and Court Binders

question: Are poly chart dividers worth the extra cost?
answer: For charts handled every day, usually yes — poly wipes clean and resists tearing, so the set outlasts several paper equivalents. For charts that mostly sit filed, paper is the better value.
topic: Poly vs. Paper Chart Dividers for Medical Records

question: Can paper chart dividers be reinforced?
answer: Yes. Every paper tab already has a clear or colored Mylar film bonded over the tab, which is where paper tabs fail first, and optional edge reinforcing protects the punched holes.
topic: Poly vs. Paper Chart Dividers for Medical Records

question: Which lasts longer in a busy clinic?
answer: Poly, by a wide margin, because the failure mode in a clinic is moisture and tearing rather than fading. Paper with Mylar closes much of the gap at a lower price.
topic: Poly vs. Paper Chart Dividers for Medical Records

question: How should I color code chart sections?
answer: Assign one color per section and use it everywhere, in every chart, without exception. The value comes from consistency, not from the palette.
topic: How to Color-Code Medical Chart Sections

question: How many colors should a chart system use?
answer: Enough that neighboring tabs are high-contrast and no two adjacent sections read as the same color at a glance. Beyond that, more colors make the system harder to remember.
topic: How to Color-Code Medical Chart Sections

question: How does the color get onto custom tabs?
answer: Colored Mylar reinforcement carries the color on paper tabs, and poly tabs are made from colored stock. Either way the color is part of the tab rather than a sticker that peels.
topic: How to Color-Code Medical Chart Sections

question: Is it worth ordering extra sets to get a lower price?
answer: Only when you will genuinely use them. The per-set price does fall with quantity, but sets that sit in a closet until the wording changes were never a saving.
topic: How Many Tab Sets Should You Order? (Honest Answer)

question: What is the smallest order I can place?
answer: At Tabzoola, twenty-five sets. That floor exists so a single project can order what it needs instead of buying years of inventory up front.
topic: How Many Tab Sets Should You Order? (Honest Answer)

question: How quickly can I reorder the same set?
answer: Your design is saved, so reordering is a matter of minutes rather than rebuilding the set from scratch — which is what makes ordering what you need today the better play.
topic: How Many Tab Sets Should You Order? (Honest Answer)

question: What is Mylar reinforcement?
answer: A thin polyester film bonded along the tab edge of a paper divider. It is the part of the tab that takes the abuse, so reinforcing it is what stops tabs tearing off.
topic: Mylar-Reinforced Tabs: What the Laminate Does

question: Do I always need Mylar reinforcement?
answer: It comes standard: every Tabzoola paper tab has Mylar on the tab, clear or colored. The optional extra is edge reinforcing along the punched edge, which earns its cost on sets handled often or kept for years.
topic: Mylar-Reinforced Tabs: What the Laminate Does

question: Should I choose clear or colored Mylar?
answer: Clear keeps the tab looking like the paper stock. Colored Mylar doubles as the color-coding system, which is why chart and case-file sets usually specify it.
topic: Mylar-Reinforced Tabs: What the Laminate Does

question: What are bottom tab dividers?
answer: Divider pages with the tab die-cut on the bottom edge instead of the side, so the titles are read straight on as you look down into the binder. Tabzoola makes them on an ordinary 8.5″ × 11″ portrait sheet; the tab hangs half an inch below the page, so the finished size is 8.5″ × 11.5″, and legal finishes 8.5″ × 14.5″. Bottom tab dividers and hanging tabs are the same product under two names.
topic: Hanging Tab Dividers — 8.5″ × 11.5″, Numbered to 150

question: Can I order bottom tab dividers numbered 1–150?
answer: Yes. The designer’s auto-fill types the whole sequence — any range up to 150 tabs per set, starting at any number, across staggered banks. Sets arrive printed, collated, and in numerical order.
topic: Hanging Tab Dividers — 8.5″ × 11.5″, Numbered to 150

question: When should I use hanging tabs instead of side tabs?
answer: Whenever the set is read from the front rather than the side — tax return sets, report covers, anything flipped down into on a desk — and always when the binding is on the top edge, since pages bound on top pivot over a side tab. If the binder is a standard left-bound 3-ring worked from the edge, use side tabs.
topic: Hanging Tab Dividers — 8.5″ × 11.5″, Numbered to 150

question: Can top-bound hanging tabs be three-hole punched?
answer: Only when the bound edge is the 11″ one. A standard US three-hole pattern needs 8.5″ between the outer hole centres, so along an 11″ edge it sits comfortably with 1.25″ to spare at each end. Along an 8.5″ edge that same span would put the outer holes exactly on the corners, so that pattern cannot be used — the short-edge standard is 2.75″ centres instead: two holes (2.875″ clear at each end) or three holes, 5.5″ between the outer centres. Tabzoola punches either pattern, and any non-standard spacing to match a specific binder, post or coil is quoted at the plant.
topic: Hanging Tab Dividers — 8.5″ × 11.5″, Numbered to 150

question: Does a legal-size set punch the same way as letter?
answer: On the bottom-tab set, yes — identically. It is bound across the 8.5″ top edge and takes the same two-hole pattern at 2.75″ centres, because the tab runs along the 8.5″ edge whatever the page length. On the side-tab set the legal sheet is actually the easier one: bound down a 14″ edge, the standard three-hole pattern leaves 2.75″ clear at each end instead of letter’s 1.25″. Legal lengthens the sheet, not the tabbed edge — which is also why a legal side-tab set buys three more inches of tab run (13″ against letter’s 10″) while a legal bottom-tab set stays at 7.5″, exactly like letter.
topic: Hanging Tab Dividers — 8.5″ × 11.5″, Numbered to 150

question: What cuts are available on bottom tabs?
answer: Every cut Tabzoola makes — 1/2 through 1/15 — on a 7.5″ working width along the bottom edge, in paper (19 Mylar colors, optional edge reinforcing) or poly (11 colors). A 1/4 cut gives four 1.88″ tabs. Letter pricing is the same as the equivalent side-tab set and shows instantly as you build.
topic: Hanging Tab Dividers — 8.5″ × 11.5″, Numbered to 150

question: Why do my binder tabs keep tearing?
answer: The tab extension is the grab point, and plain paper concentrates every pull on a half-inch of unprotected stock. Mylar reinforcement — polyester film bonded along the tab edge — is the standard fix; solid poly dividers go further and make the whole sheet tear-proof.
topic: Why Tab Dividers Fail: Six Failure Modes and the Fix for Each

question: How do I stop divider pages ripping out of the rings?
answer: Use real index stock. Dividers take more ring stress than any other page because they are turned on every visit to their section — 90 lb or 110 lb index survives it, 20 lb copy paper does not. For hard-use binders, poly holes cannot propagate a tear at all.
topic: Why Tab Dividers Fail: Six Failure Modes and the Fix for Each

question: Why don't my printed divider tabs line up with the die cut?
answer: Almost always a print setting: Fit to Page shrinks the sheet a few percent and walks every tab off position, A4 shifts the geometry, and default margins clip the tab extension. Print at 100% on letter with zero margins — or use a template drawn from real production geometry.
topic: Why Tab Dividers Fail: Six Failure Modes and the Fix for Each

question: How many tabs fit in one row before they get too small to read?
answer: About 15 is the practical ceiling for one bank. Sets with more sections should step into a second staggered bank — all tabs stay visible and readable — rather than shrinking every tab to fit one row.
topic: Why Tab Dividers Fail: Six Failure Modes and the Fix for Each

question: Are tab inserts or printed tabs more durable?
answer: Printed. An insert is a separate part that can fall out, fade, or return to the wrong slot; printing the title directly on the tab removes the part entirely. Inserts make sense only when section names genuinely change month to month.
topic: Why Tab Dividers Fail: Six Failure Modes and the Fix for Each

question: Why do paper chart dividers fall apart so fast in a clinic?
answer: Clinical handling is the worst case for paper: disinfectant wipe-downs soak the tab edge, gloved hands abrade it, and daily pulls concentrate on the same few tabs. Solid .015 poly dividers — one piece of wipeable plastic, tab included — are built for exactly that environment; Mylar-reinforced paper is the economical choice for charts that mostly sit filed.
topic: Why Medical Chart Dividers Fail: Five Clinical Failure Modes

question: What chart dividers hold up to disinfectant wipe-downs?
answer: Poly (solid plastic) dividers. The sheet and tab are one piece of .015 polyethylene, wipeable with standard surface disinfectants, with the printing fused to the plastic so section names don't rub off. Paper dividers, even reinforced, aren't made for routine wipe-downs.
topic: Why Medical Chart Dividers Fail: Five Clinical Failure Modes

question: How do we keep Volume 2 of a chart matching Volume 1?
answer: Order both from the same saved design. Custom chart divider sets reorder with identical section names, colors, positions, and cut — so a thinned or split chart assembles exactly like the original instead of from whatever the supply closet has.
topic: Why Medical Chart Dividers Fail: Five Clinical Failure Modes

question: Why did our chart color-coding stop working?
answer: Usually drift: a reorder that didn't quite match the original colors, or hand-assembled sets with shuffled positions. Once charts disagree, staff stop trusting the code. Lock each section's color in a saved custom design and order collated sets, and every chart in the building stays identical.
topic: Why Medical Chart Dividers Fail: Five Clinical Failure Modes

question: What cut should medical chart dividers be?
answer: 1/8 or 1/10 — the records-room standards. They fit a full chart's sections in one bank down the page edge while keeping each tab wide enough to read. A 1/8-cut tab is 1.25 inches; a 1/10 is 1.00 inch, on a 9 × 11 finished sheet whose tabs stay visible past the chart contents.
topic: Why Medical Chart Dividers Fail: Five Clinical Failure Modes

question: Can you write on the tabs of index dividers?
answer: Yes, on paper tabs — index stock is uncoated and takes handwriting, with permanent marker holding up better than ballpoint. Two things decide whether it stays legible: the cut (a 1/5 or 1/4 tab has room to write; a 1/10 does not) and the surface (poly's wipe-clean face is exactly what keeps ink from bonding).
topic: Write-On vs Printed Tabs — When Handwriting Is Fine, When It Costs You

question: When are write-on tabs the right choice?
answer: A binder or two whose sections keep changing, labels only you will read, or a set needed this afternoon — an office-store write-on pack is the honest answer there, and no custom order beats it on speed. Write-on stops making sense when the same labels repeat across sets.
topic: Write-On vs Printed Tabs — When Handwriting Is Fine, When It Costs You

question: Are printed tabs more expensive than writing them yourself?
answer: Usually the opposite once quantity is real. A custom-printed 8-tab paper set is $8.17/set at the 25-set minimum and $2.61/set at 250 — with the titles printed, collated in order, 3-hole punched and Mylar-reinforced on every tab. At Tabzoola, a 5-tab set is $5.45 per set at 25 and $1.57 at 250. Hand-writing the same 250 sets is 2,000 tabs of somebody's afternoon, and every set comes out different.
topic: Write-On vs Printed Tabs — When Handwriting Is Fine, When It Costs You

question: Can I get blank tabs and write on them later?
answer: Yes — blank index tabs come in any cut from 1/2 to 1/15, with Mylar on every tab and optional edge reinforcing. You can also mix in the designer: print the sections that never change and leave the rest blank to fill in by hand.
topic: Write-On vs Printed Tabs — When Handwriting Is Fine, When It Costs You

question: What are the dimensions of legal size paper?
answer: Legal size paper measures 8.5 by 14 inches, or 215.9 by 355.6 millimetres. The width is the same as letter; only the length differs, by exactly three inches.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: What is legal document size?
answer: Legal document size is 8.5 by 14 inches. The name comes from the long-standing use of the longer sheet for contracts, deeds and court filings, where the extra three inches carry more text per page and leave room for signature blocks.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: What size is legal paper in mm?
answer: Legal paper is 215.9 by 355.6 millimetres. US paper sizes are defined in inches, so the metric figures are exact conversions rather than a separate standard — which is why they are not round numbers the way A4 (210 by 297 mm) is.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: Is legal size paper the same as letter?
answer: No. Letter is 8.5 by 11 inches and legal is 8.5 by 14 inches. The width is identical, so both take the same three-hole punch, but legal is three inches longer.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: Is 8.5 x 11 paper legal or letter?
answer: 8.5 by 11 inches is letter size — the US default. Legal size is 8.5 by 14 inches.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: What size is letter paper?
answer: Letter size paper is 8.5 by 11 inches, or 215.9 by 279.4 millimetres. It is the standard US office and printer size, and the size almost every binder, index tab divider and sheet protector is built around. It is not the same as A4, which is 8.27 by 11.69 inches — narrower and slightly taller.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: What is legal size paper in inches?
answer: 8.5 by 14 inches, which is 215.9 by 355.6 millimetres.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: Why is legal paper longer than letter?
answer: The extra length lets long-form documents — contracts, leases, deeds, schedules — run further before a page break, which historically meant fewer pages to sign, initial and file. It is a US customary size; there is no metric equivalent, and A4 is neither.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: Do courts require legal or letter size paper?
answer: Most do not require legal any more. Federal appellate rules specify 8.5 by 11 inch paper for briefs, and most courts have standardized on letter — but some county courts, recorders and title companies still specify legal. Check the local rule before printing a filing set.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: Can I use letter size dividers in a legal size binder?
answer: They will fit on the rings, because both sizes are 8.5 inches wide, but every legal page will overhang the divider by three inches. If the documents are legal, the dividers should be legal.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: Does legal size cost more to print?
answer: Yes. A legal sheet is about 27 percent more paper than letter, and printing, die-cutting and finishing all price from the larger sheet. Tabzoola adds 30 percent for the legal sheet, shown as its own Sheet Size line as you build rather than buried in the per-set rate. Because the setup fee is the same either way, the order total lands about 23 to 30 percent above letter depending on quantity — $168.13 against $136.25 for 25 five-tab sets, $2,386.25 against $1,842.50 for 250 twenty-five-tab sets.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: What is the difference between legal size and A4?
answer: A4 is 8.27 by 11.69 inches (210 by 297 mm) — the international standard, close to letter. Legal, at 8.5 by 14 inches, is longer than both and is used almost exclusively in the United States.
topic: Legal Paper Size & Dimensions: 8.5 x 14 vs Letter

question: How do I print on binder tabs?
answer: Set your document to a 9 × 11 inch page with zero margins, place the tab text in the half-inch extension along the right edge rotated 90 degrees, then print at Actual Size on 90 lb index stock through the bypass tray. The four settings that most often ruin it are Fit to Page scaling, an A4 paper default, non-zero margins, and stock too heavy for the printer to feed.
topic: How to Print Binder Tabs: Word, PDF and Copier Setup

question: How do I print divider tabs in Word?
answer: Word has no divider feature, so you build the sheet: set a custom page size of 9 × 11 inches, set all four margins to zero and decline Word's offer to fix them, then insert a one-column table down the right edge with one row per tab and use Layout → Text Direction to rotate each label 90 degrees. Print at 100%, never Fit to Page.
topic: How to Print Binder Tabs: Word, PDF and Copier Setup

question: Why does my tab text print on the page instead of on the tab?
answer: Almost always because the page is set to 8.5 inches wide instead of 9, or because Word's margin warning was accepted. Both pull the text back inside the body of the sheet. The tab lives in the half inch beyond the 8.5 inch body, so the page has to be 9 inches wide and the margins have to be zero.
topic: How to Print Binder Tabs: Word, PDF and Copier Setup

question: What paper weight do I need to print binder tabs?
answer: 90 lb index is the production standard and 110 lb is stiffer; Tabzoola prints on both. 20 lb copy paper will not stand up as a tab and tears at the extension. Check your printer's maximum media weight before buying — many home and office machines stop feeding around 80 lb, which is the usual reason a template job is abandoned.
topic: How to Print Binder Tabs: Word, PDF and Copier Setup

question: Can I print on pre-cut copier tab stock?
answer: Yes, and it is easier than printing a template. Load it in the bypass or tab tray, set the driver media type to Tab Stock and the paper size to 9 × 11, and set your document to 9 × 11. If the driver offers a tab shift or offset, set it to 0.5 inches and it places the image on the extension for you. Proof one sheet before running the bank.
topic: How to Print Binder Tabs: Word, PDF and Copier Setup

question: Can I add Mylar reinforcing to tabs I print myself?
answer: No. The Mylar on a Tabzoola tab is applied on a press and the tab is then cut in the same second operation, after the sheet is printed. It is not a film that can be added to a finished sheet, which is why a home-printed tab wears at the extension in a way a Mylar-covered one does not.
topic: How to Print Binder Tabs: Word, PDF and Copier Setup

question: Is it cheaper to print my own binder tabs?
answer: For one set, yes. Across many binders the labor is what costs — index stock by the ream, hand feeding, aligning and collating — and custom printed sets, like Tabzoola's, arrive die-cut and collated in order with the labels printed on the tab itself. The threshold most people find is the third time they write the same label.
topic: How to Print Binder Tabs: Word, PDF and Copier Setup

question: What is 90 lb index stock?
answer: A stiff uncoated paper of roughly 163 gsm, made to be handled rather than read. It is the production standard for tab dividers because it holds a cut edge, takes ink well and does not curl inside a binder. The 90 lb figure is the weight of 500 sheets at index's own basis size, which is why it cannot be compared directly to 90 lb text or to 20 lb bond copy paper.
topic: Index Stock, Mylar and Die-Cutting: What They Actually Are

question: Is 110 lb index thicker than 90 lb?
answer: Yes — roughly 199 gsm against 163 gsm, about 22 percent more substance. Choose 110 lb when a set will be pulled daily for years; 90 lb is enough for most binders and is the standard.

question: What is Mylar on a tab divider?
answer: A polyester film bonded along the tab so the extension survives handling. Tabzoola applies it on a press and cuts the tab in the same second operation, so the film goes on before the cut and the edge seals as it is made. It covers the tab only, not the whole sheet, and comes in 19 colors. It is a paper option; solid poly dividers do not need it.

question: Is Mylar the same as laminating?
answer: No. Laminating encases an entire sheet in plastic. Tab Mylar is a narrow strip on the tab alone, which leaves the rest of the divider as plain paper you can still write on, and is applied before the tab is cut rather than after.

question: What does die-cutting mean?
answer: Cutting a shape with a steel rule mounted in a press, in one stroke. It is how a tab is made: a straight trimmer can only cut across a whole sheet, while a tab is a shape that stops partway along the edge. One stroke also means every sheet comes out identical, which is what makes a hundred binders match.

question: Why can a printer not just cut tabs?
answer: Two reasons. The tab extends half an inch past the 8.5 by 11 inch body, into the strip a desktop printer grips to pull the sheet, so it cannot image there. And cutting the shape needs a die rather than a straight blade. Both operations happen on a press, which is why tab dividers are a manufactured item rather than a printing job.

question: Can you write on index stock?

question: What are the California rules for exhibit tabs?

question: Does immigration court require exhibit tabs?

question: Do federal courts have a rule for exhibit tabs?
answer: Not a national one, but some federal courts do. The 11th Circuit requires indexing tabs on a paper appendix, staggered down the right-hand side and numbered with district court docket numbers; the Eastern District of Virginia and the District of Maryland require tabbed, indexed exhibits; the Central District of California and the District of Nevada require exhibits to be tabbed; the Northern District of Illinois and Southern District of Florida ban protruding tabs on paper originals. Elsewhere the judge's standing order decides.

question: Which courts do not allow tabs on filings?

CV-10(b), originals only). Texas and Kentucky appeals ban protruding tabs on the unbound copy of an appendix. Each uses a printed separator sheet instead.

question: Does a Texas appellate appendix need tabs?

question: How should tabs be placed on an 11th Circuit appendix?
